title: Odisha Rejects Premature Release of Dara Singh in Graham Staines Murder Case
excerpt: The State Sentence Review Board rejected the premature release plea on law-and-order grounds, after the Supreme Court repeatedly pressed Odisha to decide without further delay.
body:
• Odisha's State Sentence Review Board has rejected premature release for Dara Singh, also known as Rabindra Kumar Pal, who is serving life imprisonment for the 1999 murder of Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two young sons, who were burnt alive in their vehicle in Keonjhar district.
  • The decision, reported by multiple outlets including the Times of India, cites law-and-order concerns. It follows repeated Supreme Court orders directing the state to decide the plea without further delay.
  • Singh, now over 60, has spent more than 26 years in prison. He sought remission under the Odisha Premature Release Policy of 2022, arguing he has repented and invoking the principle of reformative justice.
  • The rejection lands just as the case returns to a Supreme Court bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi, which had warned that it would take its own decision if the board failed to act.

The Odisha government has rejected the plea for premature release of Dara Singh, the convict serving life imprisonment for the 1999 triple murder of Australian missionary Graham Stuart Staines and his two minor sons. The State Sentence Review Board's decision, reported on Tuesday, closes — at least for now — a remission battle that has run through five earlier review committees and landed repeatedly before the Supreme Court.

According to the Times of India, the board turned down the release on law-and-order grounds. The Hindu, Hindustan Times, ThePrint and Telegraph India carried the development the same day.

The Supreme Court's pressure

The rejection comes at the end of a bruising sequence in the top court. In July, a bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Vijay Bishnoi asked Odisha to decide Singh's plea by August 19. When that deadline passed with no decision, the bench gave the review board "one last opportunity" and orally warned that it would take its own decision at the next hearing.

https://x.com/DeccanHerald/status/2099896860865441861

In his writ petition, filed through advocate Vishnu Shankar Jain, Singh contended that he had completed more than 24 years of actual imprisonment — beyond the qualifying period under the state's premature release policy — and had never once been released on parole, not even when his mother died. He argued that continued incarceration violated his rights under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.

"Take a decision; otherwise, we will summon your officers. You have to decide one way or the other. For two years, you have been delaying the decision."

— Justice Manoj Misra, addressing the Odisha government in court

When the state sought yet another adjournment this month — its counsel citing a viral infection for the advocate-on-record — the bench refused to be put off any longer. That pressure has now produced a decision: rejection.

A crime that drew global attention

The underlying case remains one of independent India's most notorious. On the night of January 21-22, 1999, a mob led by Dara Singh set fire to the station wagon in which Graham Staines, his wife Gladys's husband and a leprosy worker in Odisha, was sleeping with his sons Philip, 10, and Timothy, 6, at Manoharpur village in Keonjhar district. All three were burnt alive.

The trial court sentenced Singh to death in 2003. The Orissa High Court commuted that to life imprisonment in 2005, holding that the case did not fall in the "rarest of rare" category — a finding the Supreme Court upheld in 2011. The apex court's own judgment recorded that the mob's intention had been "to teach a lesson to Graham Staines about his religious activities, namely, converting poor tribals to Christianity."

Singh's argument for freedom

In his remission plea, Singh said he deeply regretted what he described as transgressions committed in a "fit of youthful rage" and cited the Supreme Court's 2022 decision freeing A.G. Perarivalan, a Rajiv Gandhi assassination-case convict, as precedent for reformative justice. Five Sentence Review Committees had already examined his case over the years, rejecting remission each time — the last in February 2024. The board's latest decision keeps that streak intact.

What happens next

The matter now goes back to the Supreme Court, where the bench had previously said that if no decision were taken, the court itself would decide. Singh's legal team can challenge the rejection or ask the court to review the board's reasoning, including the law-and-order justification. Given the court's record in this case, the bench of Justices Misra and Bishnoi is unlikely to let the file rest — the next hearing will test whether the state's reasoning survives judicial scrutiny.

For now, Dara Singh remains in prison, more than 26 years after the crime that made his name synonymous with one of the darkest episodes of sectarian violence in Odisha's history.
